longForm.title: Operation Pocket Money: The Mining of Haiphong Harbor and What the Documents Show
longForm.excerpt: On May 8, 1972, Nixon announced the mining of Haiphong Harbor — a decision years in the making, timed to the Moscow Summit, and designed around a diplomatic calculation that proved correct. The Soviet Union protested. The summit proceeded on schedule.
paragraphs: The National Security Council meeting of May 8, 1972 produced a presidential decision that had been under consideration for years. Kissinger's record of the meeting notes the participants — Nixon, Kissinger, Haig, Admiral Moorer, and the secretaries of State and Defense — and the conclusion: the United States would mine Haiphong Harbor and the other principal ports of North Vietnam, and would simultaneously resume the strategic bombing campaign that had been suspended since 1968. What the meeting record does not show, but what the surrounding documentary context makes clear, is that the decision had already been shaped by a diplomatic calculation: the Moscow Summit, at which Nixon and Brezhnev were to sign the SALT I treaty, was scheduled for May 22. Nixon had concluded — and the subsequent record confirms the conclusion was correct — that the Soviet Union would not cancel a summit it had invested eighteen months of diplomacy in over the mining of a North Vietnamese port.

The classified background to that calculation is documented in the FRUS record for 1969-1976. Kissinger had conducted back-channel communications with Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin throughout the spring of 1972, gauging Soviet flexibility on Vietnam in the context of strategic arms negotiations. The Soviet position, as the cable traffic records it, was that Moscow could not openly condone American military escalation against a Soviet ally, but that the relationship's broader interests — SALT I, grain deals, trade normalization — were a separate matter from the North Vietnamese supply question. The Soviets had been providing North Vietnam with the SA-2 missiles and tanks that were sustaining the Easter Offensive, which had begun on March 30 and produced significant ARVN losses. The documentary record does not indicate that Kissinger told Dobrynin the mining was coming before May 8. It indicates that Kissinger had concluded the Soviets would swallow it.

Nixon delivered a televised address to the nation on May 8, 1972, announcing the mining of Haiphong Harbor and the other principal North Vietnamese ports. The mines being laid, he explained, were equipped with a seventy-two-hour delay fuze — sufficient time for neutral shipping already in the harbor to depart safely. The delay fuze was a legal and diplomatic gesture: it demonstrated that the United States was not attempting to sink Soviet ships, only to deny North Vietnam the port. Soviet vessels currently in Haiphong Harbor at the time of the announcement were, however, trapped for the duration; they could not leave without either waiting for the mines to be swept — which did not happen — or requesting mine-free corridors, which would have amounted to acknowledging the blockade's effectiveness. The Soviet response was a formal diplomatic protest, delivered on May 9. The Moscow Summit proceeded on schedule on May 22.

The mining of Haiphong was conducted by aircraft from the carrier USS Coral Sea, with A-6 Intruder and A-7 Corsair II aircraft laying the initial mines on the night of May 9. Thirty-six mines were placed in the harbor entrance. Operation POCKET MONEY, as it was designated, expanded over the following weeks to include the ports of Cam Pha, Hon Gai, Thanh Hoa, Vinh, Dong Hoi, and Quang Khe. The mines used were Mark 52 magnetic/acoustic combination mines, designed to be triggered by the combination of a ship's magnetic field and the acoustic signature of its propellers — making them resistant to simple magnetic sweeping. By the end of the mining campaign, approximately 11,000 mines had been placed in North Vietnamese waters. The shipping lanes that had previously been carrying an estimated 85 percent of North Vietnam's seaborne supply were closed for the duration of the operation.

The effect on North Vietnamese logistics was significant but not decisive, for the same reason that the air campaigns had not been decisive: the supply system adapted. The Ho Chi Minh Trail and the rail lines from China absorbed more of the burden that had previously moved by sea. Chinese aid to North Vietnam increased in the months following the mining. Soviet ships offloaded cargo at Chinese ports and sent it overland. The operational disruption was real — the Easter Offensive, which had made significant gains in April and May 1972, was halted in part by the combined weight of Linebacker I bombing and the supply disruption from the mining. But the disruption did not break the NVA's operational capacity; it degraded it. The distinction between a degraded and a broken adversary is the difference between an opponent who cannot achieve his current objectives and one who cannot sustain the fight at all. The mining achieved the former.

The diplomatic record of May-July 1972 shows that the mining produced exactly the Soviet response Nixon had predicted: protest without escalation. Brezhnev and Nixon signed the SALT I Interim Agreement and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty in Moscow on May 26. Kissinger's back-channel with Dobrynin continued through the summer. The North Vietnamese, whose supply lines had been disrupted and whose Easter Offensive had stalled, resumed serious negotiations in the fall of 1972. The sequence — mining in May, Linebacker I bombing through October, Paris negotiations in the fall, Linebacker II bombing in December, Paris Accords in January 1973 — has led some analysts to credit the mining with having initiated the chain of events that ended the war. The relationship is real. It is also consistent with the interpretation that the war ended because both sides had exhausted the available military options, and the mining was one of several coercive instruments applied in the final year.

The documents that are missing from the public record are instructive. The CIA's assessment of the mining's probable effect on North Vietnamese logistics, prepared before the operation, has not been fully declassified. The assessment's conclusions — to the extent they can be reconstructed from references in other documents — appear to have been more cautious about the mining's strategic effect than the public statements suggested. Kissinger's private assessments to Nixon of what the mining would and would not achieve are partially available in the FRUS record; they suggest a more modest expectation than the public address conveyed. The gap between the private assessment and the public claim is a consistent feature of the Nixon administration's handling of Vietnam policy, documented across multiple episodes from 1969 through 1972. Haiphong was not an exception.

The mines placed in Haiphong Harbor in May 1972 were swept by US Navy minesweepers following the Paris Peace Accords, in an operation that lasted from February through July 1973. Operation END SWEEP involved twelve US Navy minesweeping helicopters and surface craft working the harbor entrance over a period of five months. North Vietnamese cooperation was required and was provided, within the limits of what the after-action record describes as a cautious and adversarial working relationship. The mines that had been the most operationally effective were also the most difficult to clear — the combination magnetic/acoustic fuzing made systematic sweeping slow. The record of END SWEEP is one of the few operational chapters of the Vietnam War in which the opposing forces worked in direct proximity without shooting at each other. It has received proportionately little attention.

shortForm.title: The Moscow Summit and the Mining: Nixon's Diplomatic Gamble, May 1972
shortForm.excerpt: Nixon mined Haiphong Harbor two weeks before a summit with Brezhnev that had taken eighteen months to arrange. He calculated the Soviets would not cancel it. The FRUS record shows how that calculation was made — and what Kissinger's backchannel with Dobrynin actually said.
paragraphs: The Moscow Summit of May 22-30, 1972 had been under negotiation since 1971. It was the first visit by an American president to the Soviet Union, and its principal deliverable was SALT I — the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty that placed ceilings on intercontinental ballistic missiles and submarine-launched ballistic missiles. The Soviets had invested significant political capital in reaching SALT I, partly from genuine arms control interest and partly because the treaty framework legitimized their strategic parity with the United States. They were not going to cancel the summit over Haiphong. Nixon understood this and Kissinger had confirmed it through back-channel communications with Dobrynin. The timing of Operation POCKET MONEY — announced May 8, two weeks before the summit — was not coincidental. It was calculated.

The calculation was documented in Kissinger's backchannel communications. The relevant message traffic in the FRUS record for this period shows Kissinger probing Soviet flexibility on Vietnam through Dobrynin while simultaneously managing the SALT I endgame. The Soviet position, as Dobrynin communicated it, distinguished between Soviet obligations to North Vietnam as an ally — which required a public protest of American military actions — and Soviet interests in the broader relationship with the United States, which the summit embodied. Dobrynin did not tell Kissinger the Soviets would accept the mining. Kissinger concluded they would, based on the gap between the Soviets' public statements about Vietnam and their private communications about the summit's priority. He was right. The protest was filed. The summit opened on May 22.

What the Moscow Summit calculation also demonstrates is that Nixon and Kissinger understood the mining's effectiveness was partly coercive and partly diplomatic — it was designed to demonstrate to both Hanoi and the Soviets that the United States retained options it was willing to use, and that Soviet surface-to-air missiles and tanks supplied to North Vietnam would not deter those options. The SALT I summit, by proceeding on schedule, confirmed that assessment. Hanoi lost an argument it had been making since 1965: that Soviet and Chinese support provided a deterrent umbrella that prevented American escalation. The mining of Haiphong, with Soviet ships trapped in the harbor and the Moscow Summit proceeding anyway, was the practical refutation of that argument.

onThisDay.headline: United States Takes Control of Panama Canal Zone Construction
onThisDay.body: On May 4, 1904, the United States formally assumed control of Panama Canal Zone construction from the French Compagnie Nouvelle du Canal de Panama. The US Army Corps of Engineers oversaw the project, which would produce a strategic waterway allowing the Navy to shift forces between the Atlantic and Pacific without the 13,000-mile passage around Cape Horn — a mobility advantage that shaped American naval strategy through the twentieth century.
